title: Git Workflows & Collaboration
summary: Branching and merging are mechanics; a workflow is the convention a team agrees on so those mechanics don't collide. Learn the major branching models, the PR lifecycle, and why most large teams converge on trunk-based development.

slides.markdown:
[Branching and merging](branching-merging) tell you what git can physically do. A **workflow** is the convention a team layers on top: which branches exist, when they're created, how work moves between them, and what gate has to pass before code reaches production.

Without an agreed convention, every developer improvises their own branching scheme, and the coordination cost — who merges when, whose branch is stale, whose PR conflicts with whose — grows with team size. This topic covers the major named workflows, how the pull-request lifecycle actually works, and why the industry has been steadily converging on a simpler default than it used to.

slides.sectionTitle: Why teams need a convention at all
slides.markdown:
Git itself has no opinion on branching strategy — it's a neutral tool. Left unconstrained, a team of ten will produce ten different mental models of "where does my work go and when is it safe to merge," and the coordination cost of reconciling that shows up as exactly the problems [Branching & Merging](branching-merging) covered: stale merge bases, phantom diffs, and integration pain that scales with how long branches diverge.

A workflow is the answer to three questions every team must settle, explicitly or by accident: where does in-progress work live, what has to be true before it merges to the main line, and how does a release get cut from that main line. Different answers produce genuinely different branching models — not because one is objectively correct, but because they trade off differently between release control and integration speed.

slides.sectionTitle: Trunk-based vs GitFlow vs GitHub Flow
slides.markdown:
| | Trunk-based | GitFlow | GitHub Flow |
|---|---|---|
| Long-lived branches | Just `main` | `main` + `develop`, plus release/hotfix | Just `main` |
| Feature branch lifespan | Hours, merged constantly | Can live for a full release cycle | Days, merged via PR |
| How unfinished work ships | Hidden behind feature flags | Stays on `develop` until release | Stays on the feature branch until merged |
| Release mechanism | Tag `main` directly, or a short-lived release branch | Dedicated `release/*` branch, merged to both `main` and `develop` | Deploy from `main` after merge |
| Best fit | Continuous deployment, high release cadence | Scheduled releases, multiple versions in support simultaneously | Web apps deploying straight from `main` |

GitFlow was designed for a world of infrequent, versioned releases (desktop software, libraries with support branches). Trunk-based and GitHub Flow both assume you deploy far more often, and both keep exactly one long-lived branch — the difference between them is mostly ceremony around the PR, not branch topology.

GitFlow names five branch types, each with a fixed role:

- **`main`** — always reflects production; only release/hotfix branches merge into it.
- **`develop`** — the integration branch; features merge here first.
- **`feature/*`** — branched from `develop`, merged back into `develop` when done.
- **`release/*`** — branched from `develop` when preparing a release; only bugfixes land here; merges into both `main` and `develop` when shipped.
- **`hotfix/*`** — branched directly from `main` for an urgent production fix; merges into both `main` and `develop`.

The structure exists to let "what's being developed," "what's about to ship," and "what's live" stay separate at all times — valuable when releases are infrequent and multiple versions need parallel support, but it's a lot of ceremony for a team that deploys many times a day.

slides.subTitle: The modern default at scale
slides.markdown:
Trunk-based development's core rule: everyone merges small, frequent changes directly into one shared branch (`main`/`trunk`), often multiple times a day, and long-lived feature branches essentially don't exist.

The obvious problem this creates — how do you merge unfinished work into the branch everyone deploys from — is solved by **feature flags**: the code merges and deploys, but sits behind a runtime toggle that keeps it invisible or inert until the feature is actually ready. This decouples "merged" from "released," which is the opposite of GitFlow's model where merging to `main` and releasing are close to the same event.

Companies operating at very high deploy frequency (many deploys per day, per engineer even) rely on this almost universally, because it keeps every branch's divergence from `main` measured in hours, not weeks — which is exactly what keeps merge conflicts small, per [Branching & Merging](branching-merging).

Almost every modern workflow, regardless of branching model, routes changes through the same PR (pull request) / MR (merge request) lifecycle:

1. **Draft** — work in progress, visible for early feedback but not ready for a real review pass.
2. **Ready for review** — the author signals it's complete; reviewers are requested, often automatically via CODEOWNERS.
3. **CI gate** — automated checks (tests, linting, build) must pass; most platforms block merging until they do.
4. **Review** — humans read the diff, leave comments, request changes or approve; iteration continues until approved.
5. **Merge** — via whichever mode the repo enforces (merge commit, squash, rebase-and-merge), typically deleting the source branch afterward.

The PR is doing two jobs at once: it's the unit of code review, and it's the checkpoint where CI proves the change is safe to combine with everyone else's. Skipping either — merging without review, or bypassing a failing CI gate — is how broken code reaches the shared branch.

slides.sectionTitle: Merge commit vs squash vs rebase-and-merge on a PR
slides.markdown:
PR platforms typically expose three merge buttons, each producing a different shape on the shared branch:

| Mode | What lands on the target branch |
|---|---|
| **Merge commit** | Every commit from the PR, plus one new two-parent merge commit |
| **Squash and merge** | One new commit containing the PR's combined diff; individual commits are discarded |
| **Rebase and merge** | Every commit from the PR, replayed with new hashes directly onto the target branch, no merge commit |

Squash is the most common default for typical feature PRs — it keeps the shared branch linear without needing anyone to manually clean up commits first. Rebase-and-merge gives the same linear result while preserving individual commits, at the cost of every commit's hash changing (which can trigger re-review on some platforms). Full merge commits are reserved for PRs where the granular commit history is itself worth keeping.

Even trunk-based teams sometimes need a way to patch what's already live without shipping everything currently sitting on `main`. A **hotfix** branches directly from the last release's exact commit (or a tag), applies only the urgent fix, and ships from there — bypassing whatever half-finished work has since landed on `main` behind feature flags.

A **release branch** serves a similar purpose at larger scale: cut it from `main` when preparing a release, and only bugfixes land on it afterward, while `main` keeps moving for the next cycle. This matters when a team supports multiple live versions simultaneously (an SDK with LTS versions, an on-prem product several customers haven't upgraded) — each supported version gets its own release branch to receive fixes without needing the entire codebase frozen.

The trade-off is real: every additional long-lived branch is another place a fix has to be replicated to (cherry-picked or reapplied), and teams that support many versions in parallel invest real tooling in tracking which fixes have landed where.

slides.subTitle: How branching and ownership change with repo shape
slides.markdown:
| | Monorepo (one repo, many projects) | Polyrepo (one repo per project) |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-project changes | One atomic commit/PR across everything | Coordinated PRs across multiple repos, no atomicity |
| Branching model | Usually trunk-based by necessity, at real scale | Each repo can pick its own workflow independently |
| Ownership | Path-based (CODEOWNERS), everyone shares one branch | Repo boundary *is* the ownership boundary |
| CI cost | Every commit can trigger a huge build graph unless scoped | Each repo's CI is naturally scoped to itself |
| Dependency versioning | Usually always-latest, in the same commit | Explicit version pins across repo boundaries |

Monorepos remove an entire class of cross-repo coordination problems (a shared library change and its consumers land atomically) but demand serious tooling investment — sparse checkouts, build graph scoping, path-based CI — to stay usable at scale, covered further in [Git at Scale](git-at-scale). Polyrepos keep each team's tooling independent at the cost of every cross-cutting change becoming a multi-repo coordination exercise.

slides.sectionTitle: Long-lived feature branches causing merge debt
slides.markdown:
The most common workflow failure isn't picking the wrong named model — it's letting feature branches live far longer than the workflow assumes. A GitHub Flow branch meant to merge in a day or two that instead survives for six weeks accumulates exactly the integration pain [Branching & Merging](branching-merging) describes: a stale merge base, an enormous diff, and conflicts across files that changed for unrelated reasons.

Teams call the accumulated version of this **merge debt** — the growing gap between a branch and the shared trunk that gets more expensive to close the longer it's deferred, the same way technical debt compounds. It typically happens for understandable reasons: a feature genuinely isn't ready, so nobody wants to merge "broken" code — but the fix is a feature flag, not a longer-lived branch. Merging early and hiding incompleteness behind a flag keeps the branch's actual git lifetime short, regardless of how long the feature itself takes to finish.

slides.subTitle: The senior-level nuance
slides.markdown:
A workflow's real strength isn't the branch diagram — it's what's actually required before code reaches the shared branch, and that's a deliberate design decision, not a default.

Strong CI gates typically require, at minimum: the full test suite passing, a build succeeding, and at least one human approval, often via CODEOWNERS routing so the right domain expert reviews the right path. Weaker setups skip one of these under time pressure — allowing merges on a red build "just this once" — and that exception becomes the norm the moment it happens without consequence.

The workflow decision that separates senior engineering judgment from cargo-culting a named model: which gate is worth the friction for *this* codebase. A payments system justifies mandatory two-approval review and a full integration suite on every PR; an internal tools repo with low blast radius might reasonably relax to single-approval and a faster subset of tests. The named workflow (trunk-based, GitFlow) is the branch topology; the gates are the actual safety mechanism, and they need to be tuned to risk, not copied from another team's README.

Workflows describe how work is *supposed* to flow. Mistakes still happen inside any of them — a bad merge, a commit that shouldn't have landed, a branch that needs to be reverted entirely. The next topic, **Undoing Changes & Recovery**, covers the tools for fixing those mistakes safely, at every stage from an unstaged edit to a commit that's already been pushed.
